title: The long story of a past Buddha (Kern ch. 7)
word: The long story of a past Buddha
hook: a Buddha of ages past and his sixteen sons who taught

segments.voice: Yesterday, vyakarana: like starving men at a royal meal, the great disciples heard the Buddha name each one's future. Your line: a future foretold.

Chapter seven of the Lotus looks back, so far back that the sutra needs a whole picture just to say how long ago. The Diamond Sutra ground a world to dust to ask what a heap is. The Lotus grinds a world to dust to measure time. Carry the dust across the worlds, and let fall one speck only after crossing a great stretch of them, until the dust is gone. The time since this story is longer than that.
screen: `FROM FUTURES TO THE PAST.` → `DUST THAT MEASURES TIME.` → `LONGER AGO THAN THAT.`

segments.voice: Kern gives the old Buddha's name as Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu. He sat at the seat of awakening, and for a long time full awakening did not come. He stayed seated, steady, until at last it did. Before he left home, the story says, he had been a prince with sixteen sons. When they heard their father had awakened, they left their toys and palaces to honor him, their family following behind, and asked him to teach. Kings of the heavens came too, from every direction, offering their palaces and asking the same. Their father taught the early teachings first, and many were freed. Later the sixteen sons, now young monks, asked him for more, and he taught them this very sutra, the Lotus. Then he went into a long meditation, and while he sat, each son took a seat and taught the Lotus to the crowds, in detail, for a long time. Here is the turn. Those sixteen sons, the Buddha says, are all Buddhas now, teaching in different directions. One of them, in the west, is called Amitayus. And the sixteenth son is me. I am the one who taught you then. The listeners in front of him today are the same beings he taught as that young monk, ages ago. The long story isn't a detour. It tells the disciples why they are here. The teaching has a lineage older than they can picture, passed from father to sons, from sons to listeners, and they were already in it. Yesterday's promises weren't new. They were old seeds coming up.
screen: `A BUDDHA OF AGES PAST.` · `A PRINCE WITH SIXTEEN SONS.` · `THE SONS TEACH THE LOTUS.` · `THE SIXTEENTH SON IS ME.` · then, large: `SIXTEEN SONS.`

segments.voice: Think of something you know how to do, a craft, a song, a recipe, a way of praying or sitting, and ask who taught it to you, then who taught them. Follow the chain back, face by face, until the faces blur. Rest at the edge of what you can see, grateful to everyone in the line, known and unknown.
The long story of a past Buddha. In chapter seven, a Buddha of ages past teaches the Lotus to his sixteen sons; the sixteenth is the Buddha telling the story. Today's word.
screen: `THE LONG STORY OF A PAST BUDDHA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: sixteen sons. The teacher in the story was the teacher telling it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Lotus Sutra readers in East Asia study chapter seven's story of the ancient Buddha and his sixteen sons as the account of the Buddha's long bond with his hearers; some readers link the mention of Amitayus in the west to Pure Land devotion.

chat.says: Why does the Lotus Sutra tell such a long story about a Buddha from ages ago?
options: He was the sixteenth son who taught these same listeners back then, so they were already in it.
To show that this old Buddha was greater than the one now teaching on the mountain.
To explain why the sixteen sons never became Buddhas and had to start over.
chat.meaning: In chapter seven the Buddha says he was the sixteenth son, and his listeners are the ones he taught then: an old lineage, not a detour.

Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu.meaning: the Buddha of ages past in chapter seven, as Kern spells it

Diamond Sutra.meaning: a short Mahayana sutra that cuts through every grip

Kern.meaning: the scholar whose English translation of the Lotus this path follows

notes: Chapter 7 paraphrased from Kern (SBE XXI, 1884); nothing quoted.

Check: the dust-of-a-world image for the length of time (Kern gives specific counts, omitted); the name Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu as Kern spells it; the delay before full awakening (Kern gives a number of intermediate ages, omitted); the sons' family following them (Kumarajiva has mothers and the grandfather-king; simplified to 'their family'); the Brahma kings from the directions; the sixteen sons as novices teaching while their father was in meditation; Amitayus/Amitabha in the west and Shakyamuni as the sixteenth.
The phrase 'old seeds coming up' is an image, not a quoted term.
Original: Purvayoga (पूर्वयोग); Kern renders the chapter title along the lines of 'ancient devotion'; check.
